The taxpayer completing this study is Susteon Inc. This LCA report has been prepared in accordance with ISO 14040/14044 requirements and with the NETL CO2U LCA Guidance Document as modified by the 45Q addendum. This report details the results of the life cycle assessment and demonstrates the net CO reduction due to 2 Susteon’s Direct Air Capture (DAC) process as part of project DE-FE0032254, “Bench-Scale Development of Promoted High-Capacity Structured Sorbents.” Since the captured CO from Susteon’s DAC technology 2 will be sent to saline storage for permanent sequestration, the LCA is conducted on a cradle-to-grave basis from capturing CO to permanent storage. 2 The system under study is a facility with a nominal CO capture rate of 100,000 tonnes per year (TPY) with 2 a capacity factor of 85%. This study was conducted as a cradle-to-grave analysis normalized to the basis of 1 kg CO captured from the atmosphere and permanently stored in a saline aquifer. Moreover, the study 2 considers the CO emissions associated with the extraction of raw materials, processing of said raw 2 materials, electricity, and other consumables used for the DAC process, on-site activity, and transportation and storage against the CO that was captured by the DAC process where possible. Figure 1 shows the 2 system boundary and all the elements considered in this LCA. Figure 1: Susteon’s DAC Process’ System Boundary The streams flowing in and out of the system boundary were implemented within an openLCA model to generate the openLCA model graph as shown in Figure 2. A previous life cycle assessment for this technology indicated that the electricity-intensity of the DAC process is the main driver of overall GWP of the process. As such, a comparative LCA was performed to show the impact of the electricity mix on the overall global warming potential of the CO captured and stored via the DAC process at its current 2 5 LCA: DE-FE0032254 development state. Four electricity sources, listed below and shown in the system model (Figure 2, Figure 11), were evaluated in the comparative LCA: 1. Fossil power with carbon capture and storage (CCS) 2. 2050 U.S. grid mix 3. Current U.S. grid mix 4.
